pages.html:

5th Grade PE · Unit 1.1 · Intro to P.E.
Week 1

Welcome, Athlete in Training 🏅

You've been moving for as long as you can remember — running on the playground, biking, dancing, climbing. By 5th grade, your body is more capable than ever. This year, Mission: Move! treats you like the athlete you're becoming: someone who trains on purpose, understands how your body works, and uses that knowledge to get stronger.

1
Lesson 1
Why Physical Activity Matters

Physical activity is any movement that gets your heart pumping and your muscles working. It includes obvious things like sports and PE, but also walking the dog, raking leaves, riding bikes, or dancing in your room. Health experts recommend kids your age get at least 60 minutes of activity every day — and not all in one stretch.

Why so much? Because 5th grade is the start of a huge growth window. Your bones are getting denser, your heart is getting bigger, and the wiring between your brain and muscles is being built. Movement is the signal that tells your body to build that hardware well.

2
Lesson 2
What Happens Inside When You Move

Let's open the hood. When you exercise, several body systems run at the same time:

❤️
Cardiovascular System
Your heart, blood, and vessels — they move oxygen and nutrients to working muscles.
🫁
Respiratory System
Your lungs trade oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. Faster breathing = more fuel.
💪
Muscular System
Over 600 muscles produce the force that moves your bones.
🦴
Skeletal System
206 bones give your body shape and let muscles pull against a frame.
🧠
Nervous System
Your brain sends electrical signals through nerves to tell your muscles what to do.
🧪Sport Science

Your heart beats about 100,000 times every day, pumping roughly 2,000 gallons of blood. During hard exercise, your heart rate can climb from about 70 beats per minute (resting) to 180 or more. The blood it sends out carries oxygen to your muscles. The more efficient that delivery system gets, the longer you can keep moving without slowing down. That efficiency is called your aerobic capacity.

3
Lesson 3
How Movement Helps Your Brain

Exercise isn't just a body thing. When you move, your brain releases chemicals called endorphins that lift your mood and help you handle stress. Physical activity also boosts BDNF — a protein that helps brain cells grow and connect.

Kids who are active most days of the week tend to:

  • Focus better in class
  • Remember more of what they read
  • Fall asleep faster and sleep deeper
  • Feel calmer when something stressful happens
💡Did You Know?

Brain scans show that students who exercise before school have more activity in their prefrontal cortex — the part of the brain you use for paying attention, solving problems, and making good decisions. That's why a quick movement break can help when you're stuck on hard math.

4
Lesson 4
Movement Builds Teammates and Leaders

PE also trains skills you can't measure with a stopwatch: how to communicate, how to lose without quitting, how to lift teammates up. These are sometimes called character skills, and athletes work on them just like they work on speed and strength.

Every time you join a game, you practice:

  • Cooperation — adjusting your plan to fit teammates
  • Sportsmanship — being honest about rules and respectful to opponents
  • Communication — calling for the ball, supporting a missed shot
  • Resilience — keeping your effort up after a setback
🌎Real-World Connection

Pro athletes — from Simone Biles to LeBron James — say their mental game is just as important as their physical training. Coaches at the highest level dedicate hours to teamwork, communication, and handling pressure. The reps you put in during a 5th grade game are the same reps a pro puts in.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Physical activity — Any movement that uses your muscles and burns energy.
  • Cardiovascular system — Heart, blood, and blood vessels — your body's delivery network.
  • Aerobic capacity — How well your body uses oxygen during long-duration activity.
  • Endorphins — Brain chemicals released during exercise that boost mood and reduce pain.
  • BDNF — A protein that helps brain cells grow — released during exercise (stretch term).
  • Stamina — How long you can keep working before fatigue sets in.
📝Weekly Reflection

Why does movement matter to you? List two ways physical activity helps your body and one way it helps your brain. Then answer: how do you know exercise affects your mood? Give one piece of evidence from your own life (a time you felt better after moving, or worse when you skipped it).

Flight Club

Flight Club Guidelines 🦉

Welcome to the Flight Club — the place where you take what you've learned and put it to the test. Every other week, a new movement challenge drops. You complete it, record it (or describe it), and earn Flight Club points. Here's how it works.

1
Mission
What Flight Club Is

Flight Club is the active part of Mission: Move!. Each module ends with a Flight Club challenge — a short, focused movement task connected to that module's topic. It's where the lesson meets the doing.

Some challenges train strength. Some train endurance. Some train coordination or sportsmanship. They're designed to take 5–15 minutes and require minimal equipment.

2
Rules
Flight Club Rules
  1. Read the full challenge first. Know what you're doing before you start.
  2. Warm up. 2–3 minutes of light cardio + dynamic stretches.
  3. Follow the steps in order. Don't skip — the order matters.
  4. Modify, don't quit. If a move is too hard, reduce reps or scale it down. If it's too easy, add reps.
  5. Cool down. 2–3 minutes of slow movement + static stretches.
  6. Hydrate — water before, during, after.
  7. Submit your proof. A photo, video, or written reflection — whatever the challenge asks for.
3
Crew
What Is the Flight Crew Check-In?

At the end of every challenge, you'll find a Flight Crew Check-In — two short reflection questions. Don't skip them. Real athletes train their thinking as much as their bodies. The Check-In asks you to notice what you did, why it worked (or didn't), and what you'd do differently next time.

Strong reflections earn extra Flight Club credit.

4
Safety
Safety First, Always
  • Check your space — clear of clutter, enough room to move
  • Wear safe shoes (closed-toe with grip)
  • Stop if something hurts beyond normal effort
  • Tell a trusted adult if you're unsure about a move
💡Did You Know?

Pro athletes call recovery and self-review "the secret 1%". They spend 80% of their time training, 19% in competition — and that final 1% reflecting on what worked. It's the smallest slice, but it's what separates good athletes from great ones. The Flight Crew Check-In is your 1%.

→What's Next

Ready? Your first Flight Club starts in Module 1.1, Week 2. Bring your A-game.

pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
5th Grade PE · Unit 1.2 · Warm-Ups & Cool-Downs
Week 3

Warm-Ups & Cool-Downs: Prep Your Athletic Machine 🛠️

Your body is an athletic machine — and like every machine, it works best when it's properly turned on and properly turned off. A real warm-up does more than "loosen you up." It changes the chemistry of your muscles, the way your blood flows, and even how fast your brain can react. Skip it, and you train at half power. Skip the cool-down, and you pay for it tomorrow.

1
Lesson 1
What a Warm-Up Actually Does

A warm-up is a planned set of low-intensity movements done before a workout. It raises your core body temperature by about 1–2 degrees, gets your heart rate up gradually, and lubricates your joints with a substance called synovial fluid. Warm muscles stretch farther without tearing and produce force faster.

A good warm-up has two parts:

  • General warm-up — 3–5 minutes of light cardio (jogging, jumping jacks) to raise heart rate
  • Dynamic warm-up — controlled movements (arm circles, high knees, leg swings) that move your joints through their full range
🧪Sport Science

Dynamic stretching (moving while you stretch) is different from static stretching (holding a position). Research shows dynamic stretching before activity actually improves performance, while long static stretches before sprinting can reduce power. That's why coaches save the long holds for the cool-down.

2
Lesson 2
What a Cool-Down Actually Does

A cool-down is the opposite — a 5–10 minute slow-down period after activity. It gradually drops your heart rate, prevents blood from pooling in your legs (which can make you feel dizzy), and helps your body clear waste products from your muscles.

A complete cool-down includes:

  • Light movement — walking or easy jogging for 2–3 minutes
  • Static stretches — gentle holds for 15–30 seconds per muscle group
  • Deep breathing — to bring your nervous system out of "go mode"
💡Did You Know?

When you exercise hard, your muscles release a byproduct called lactate. For years, people blamed lactate for next-day soreness — but scientists have learned that lactate is actually a fuel your body recycles. The soreness comes from tiny stretches and tears in muscle fibers. Cool-downs help blood carry repair signals to those fibers faster, which can reduce how stiff you feel the next morning.

3
Try It
5 Dynamic Warm-Up Moves
💪
Arm Circles
10 forward, 10 backward — opens shoulder joints.
🦵
High Knees
20 seconds — lifts heart rate, warms hip flexors.
🔄
Leg Swings
10 per leg, forward and side — wakes up hamstrings and adductors.
🦶
Walking Lunges
10 steps — activates quads and glutes.
🏃
Light Jog
60 seconds in place — pulls everything together.
4
Try It
5 Cool-Down Stretches
🧘
Standing Toe Touch
Hold 20s — hamstrings and lower back.
🦩
Quad Stretch
Pull one heel toward your glute, 15s per side.
🦋
Butterfly Stretch
Sit with soles together, gently press knees down. 30s.
🤸
Shoulder Stretch
Pull one arm across your chest, 15s per side.
🌬️
Deep Breaths
5 slow breaths — in through nose, out through mouth.
🌎Real-World Connection

Every professional sports team — NBA, MLB, Olympic teams — has athletic trainers whose entire job is designing warm-ups and recovery routines. A pro soccer team's pre-game warm-up can last 30 minutes. That tells you how much real athletes value this part. They don't skip it, and neither should you.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Warm-up — Low-intensity movements done before activity to prepare the body.
  • Cool-down — Slow-down movements done after activity to safely return to rest.
  • Dynamic stretching — Stretching while moving — best before activity.
  • Static stretching — Holding a stretch in one position — best after activity.
  • Range of motion — How far a joint can move comfortably (stretch term).
  • Lactate — A substance your body produces and recycles during hard exercise (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Did you actually warm up before activity this week? Compare two PE sessions — one where you warmed up properly and one where you didn't. How did your body feel different? What evidence do you have that the warm-up helped (faster, less sore, more focused)?

→What's Next

Next: design your own warm-up + cool-down routine in this week's VR assignment, then test it in Flight Club.

pages.html:

Mission: Move!
5th Grade PE · Unit 1.3 · Muscular Strength & Endurance
Week 5

Muscular Strength & Endurance: Build the Engine 💪

Strength and endurance sound similar, but they're two different skills. Strength is how hard your muscles can push or pull once. Endurance is how many times you can do it before they quit. Every athlete needs both — and the way you train each is different.

1
Lesson 1
Strength vs. Endurance

Muscular strength is the maximum amount of force a muscle can produce in a single effort. Lifting a heavy box, pushing a stuck door, or jumping as high as you can — those use strength.

Muscular endurance is how long a muscle can keep producing force without getting tired. Holding a plank for two minutes, doing 30 push-ups in a row, or carrying groceries up the stairs — those use endurance.

Imagine your bicep is a battery. Strength is the maximum power that battery can put out in one second. Endurance is how long the battery lasts before it dies.

2
Lesson 2
Major Muscle Groups

Your body has hundreds of muscles, but PE focuses on the big ones — the muscle groups that move you through space:

🦵
Quads
Front of your thighs — straighten the knee. Powers jumping and sprinting.
🦵
Hamstrings
Back of your thighs — bend the knee. Helps you decelerate and run.
🍑
Glutes
Your butt muscles — the strongest muscle group in your body. Power for running and jumping.
🎯
Core
Abs, obliques, and lower back — keep your spine stable when you move.
💪
Biceps & Triceps
Bend and straighten the elbow. Used for pulling and pushing.
🪶
Lats
Wide back muscles — power pull-ups, climbing, and swimming strokes.
🧪Sport Science

When you train a muscle, you actually create microscopic tears in its fibers. During recovery (mostly while you sleep), your body repairs those tears and adds extra protein — making the muscle slightly bigger and stronger than before. This process is called muscle protein synthesis. It's the reason rest days matter as much as training days.

3
Lesson 3
Training Strength vs. Training Endurance

The number of reps and how heavy the resistance is decides which one you're building:

  • Strength training — heavier resistance, fewer reps (3–6). Think: a few heavy push-ups against the wall.
  • Endurance training — lighter resistance, more reps (12–25+). Think: 30 bodyweight squats in a row.

Both are important. A soccer player needs endurance to run for a full game and strength to win battles for the ball. A swimmer needs endurance for long laps and strength for the dive off the wall.

💡Did You Know?

The strongest muscle in your body — for its size — is your masseter (the muscle that closes your jaw). It can produce up to 200 pounds of force on your back teeth! Your largest and most powerful muscle group, though, is your gluteus maximus — the muscle that lets you stand up, climb stairs, and sprint.

4
Try It
Bodyweight Strength Moves

You don't need weights to train strength — your own body is enough. Try this circuit:

🦾
Push-Ups
10 reps. Works chest, shoulders, triceps, and core.
🏋️
Squats
15 reps. Trains quads, glutes, and hamstrings together.
🪜
Plank Hold
30 seconds. Builds core endurance.
🌉
Glute Bridges
12 reps. Targets the glutes and lower back.
🌎Real-World Connection

Strength training isn't just for athletes — it helps everyone. Firefighters need it to carry equipment. Nurses need it to lift patients. Carpenters need it to swing hammers all day. Even adults who sit at desks train strength so they can stay healthy as they age. The strength you build now is part of your body's foundation for life.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Muscular strength — The maximum force a muscle can produce in a single effort.
  • Muscular endurance — How long a muscle can produce force before getting tired.
  • Rep (repetition) — One complete cycle of an exercise (one push-up, one squat).
  • Quads, hamstrings, glutes — The three main muscle groups in your legs.
  • Core — The muscles in your trunk that stabilize your spine.
  • Muscle protein synthesis — How muscles rebuild stronger after exercise (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Which is more important in your favorite activity — strength or endurance? Pick one sport, hobby, or game you play. Explain which fitness component you'd train more of, and why. How do you know? Give one example from how the activity is actually played.

→What's Next

Next: showcase your strength in this week's assignment, then test your endurance in Flight Club.

pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
5th Grade PE · Unit 1.4 · Cardiovascular Fitness
Week 7

Cardiovascular Fitness: Train Your Heart 🫀

Your heart is a muscle — and like every muscle, it gets stronger when you train it. Cardiovascular fitness is how well your heart, lungs, and blood vessels work together to deliver oxygen to your body. The better that delivery system, the longer you can keep moving without slowing down. This is the engine behind almost every sport.

1
Lesson 1
The Cardiovascular System, Explained

Your cardiovascular system is a closed loop made of three parts:

  • Heart — a fist-sized pump that beats around 100,000 times a day
  • Blood vessels — arteries carry oxygen-rich blood out, veins carry it back; capillaries are the tiny vessels where the swap happens
  • Blood — carries oxygen, nutrients, and carries away waste like carbon dioxide

When you breathe in, your lungs pull oxygen out of the air. Your heart pumps that oxygen-loaded blood out to working muscles. The muscles use the oxygen to make energy. The heart pumps the now low-oxygen blood back to the lungs to reload. Loop complete.

🧪Sport Science

Athletes have a measurable number called VO₂ max — the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use during all-out exercise. Distance runners and cyclists have some of the highest VO₂ max numbers ever recorded. Tour de France winners can be more than twice as efficient at using oxygen as the average adult. The good news: VO₂ max improves with training, especially when you start young.

2
Lesson 2
Aerobic vs. Anaerobic

Not all cardio is the same. There are two main fuel systems:

  • Aerobic ("with oxygen") — Moderate activity you can sustain for a long time. Examples: jogging, biking, swimming laps. Your breathing is faster but steady. You could hold a short conversation.
  • Anaerobic ("without oxygen") — Short bursts of all-out effort. Examples: sprinting, jumping for a rebound, racing to home base. You can't keep this up for long — usually under a minute.

Most sports use both. A basketball player jogs down the court (aerobic), then sprints for a fast break (anaerobic), then jogs back. Training one helps the other, but they're trained differently.

3
Lesson 3
Heart Rate & Target Zones

You can check how hard your heart is working by measuring your heart rate — beats per minute (BPM). Place two fingers on your wrist or neck, count beats for 10 seconds, multiply by 6.

  • Resting heart rate — usually 70–110 BPM for a 5th grader at rest
  • Target zone during exercise — roughly 130–170 BPM for moderate activity
  • Max heart rate — estimated as 220 minus your age (so ~210 for a 10-year-old)

You don't need to be in the top zone all the time. Most of your training should be in the moderate zone — fast enough that you can't sing, but slow enough that you could still say a sentence.

💡Did You Know?

Trained endurance athletes can have a resting heart rate as low as 40 BPM — about half the rate of an average adult. That doesn't mean their heart is weak. It means each beat pumps so much blood that the heart doesn't need to fire as often. A stronger heart works less hard at rest.

4
Try It
Cardio Training Options
🏃
Jogging
5–20 min of steady pace — classic aerobic training.
🚴
Biking
Low-impact way to build aerobic endurance.
⚡
Sprint Intervals
8× (20 sec all-out, 40 sec walk). Anaerobic + aerobic mix.
🏊
Swimming
Full-body cardio with almost no joint stress.
🪜
Stair Climbing
Builds heart strength + leg power.
💃
Dance
Yes — high-energy dance counts as serious cardio.
🌎Real-World Connection

Cardio fitness isn't just about sports — it's one of the strongest predictors of long-term health. Adults with high cardiovascular fitness live longer, get sick less often, and recover faster from injury. The habits you build at age 10 set up your heart for the next 70+ years.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Cardiovascular fitness — How well your heart, lungs, and blood vessels deliver oxygen.
  • Aerobic — Steady, moderate-intensity exercise that uses oxygen as fuel.
  • Anaerobic — Short bursts of all-out effort that don't use oxygen as the main fuel.
  • Heart rate — Beats per minute — a measure of how hard your heart is working.
  • Target zone — The heart rate range where cardio training is most effective.
  • VO₂ max — Your body's maximum rate of oxygen use (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

What does cardio fitness feel like in your body? After this week's hardest activity, what changed: breathing, heart rate, sweat, how your legs felt? How do you know your heart and lungs were working harder than at rest? Describe at least two pieces of evidence.

→What's Next

5th Grade PE · Unit 1.5 · Flexibility & Stretching
Week 9

Flexibility & Stretching: Train Your Range 🤸

Flexibility is the ability of your muscles and joints to move through their full range of motion. It sounds quiet compared to strength or speed, but it's the foundation of every other skill. The athlete who can't reach can't catch. The runner who can't extend can't sprint. Train your range, and everything else gets better.

1
Lesson 1
What Flexibility Actually Means

Your bones move because muscles pull on them. Each muscle attaches across one or more joints. When a muscle is short and tight, the joint can't move very far. When a muscle is long and supple, the joint moves freely.

Flexibility isn't just about being able to touch your toes. It's about whether your joints can do the work your sport asks of them. A pitcher needs flexible shoulders. A goalkeeper needs flexible hips. A dancer needs flexibility almost everywhere.

2
Lesson 2
Active vs. Passive Flexibility

Sport scientists describe two kinds of flexibility:

  • Active flexibility — how far you can move a joint using only your own muscles. Example: lifting your leg as high as you can without grabbing it.
  • Passive flexibility — how far the joint can move with outside help (a partner, gravity, or your hands pulling it). Example: lying on your back and pulling your leg toward your chest.

Active flexibility is what you actually use in sports. Passive flexibility is usually greater, but you can't always access it during a game. Training builds both — but most coaches focus on active range first.

🧪Sport Science

Inside your muscles are sensors called muscle spindles. When you stretch a muscle quickly, these sensors fire a reflex that tells the muscle to contract — to protect it from tearing. That's why slow, controlled stretches work better than fast bouncy ones. Hold a stretch for 15–30 seconds and the reflex relaxes, letting the muscle truly lengthen.

3
Lesson 3
Dynamic vs. Static Stretching

You already saw these in the warm-up unit — flexibility training uses both, but at different times:

  • Dynamic stretching — moving stretches done before activity. Wakes up muscles, improves performance.
  • Static stretching — holding a position after activity. Best for building long-term flexibility.

For real flexibility gains, static stretching done 3–5 times a week for at least 4 weeks is what creates lasting change. One stretch session won't change much. A habit will.

4
Try It
5 Core Static Stretches
🦋
Butterfly
Sit, soles together, press knees down. Targets inner thighs.
🦩
Flamingo
Stand on one leg, pull other heel to glute. Stretches quad.
🫳
Toe Touch
Stand, slowly reach toward toes. Hamstrings + lower back.
🐶
Downward Dog
Hands and feet on floor, hips up. Calves, hamstrings, shoulders.
🦴
Cobra
Lie face down, press chest up. Opens up the front of your body.
💡Did You Know?

Gymnasts and ballet dancers don't just have naturally flexible bodies — most started training before age 6 and stretch for 1–2 hours every single day. That's how much consistent work it takes to reach the splits or do a backbend. The lesson: flexibility is earned, not gifted. Even a small daily routine can make a noticeable difference in a few weeks.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Flexibility — The ability of a muscle or joint to move through its full range.
  • Range of motion — How far a joint can move comfortably.
  • Active flexibility — Range you can reach using only your own muscles.
  • Passive flexibility — Range you can reach with outside help (stretch term).
  • Hamstrings — The big muscles at the back of your thighs (a common tightness spot).
  • Muscle spindle — Sensor inside a muscle that protects it from being overstretched (stretch term).
🌎Real-World Connection

NFL kickers stretch their hip flexors for 20+ minutes before every game — because if their hip can't fully extend, they can't kick at full power. NBA centers spend hours weekly working on hip and ankle mobility so they can land safely from jumps. The pros don't skip stretching, and they didn't get to the pros by skipping it either.

📝Weekly Reflection

How flexible are you right now? Pick one stretch from this lesson (toe touch is a good test). Try it today, then again in two weeks after some daily practice. Which body part felt the tightest? Why do you think that area is tight — sitting too much, playing a sport that doesn't stretch it, or something else?

→What's Next

pages.title: Week 11: Nutrition
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
5th Grade PE · Unit 1.6 · Nutrition
Week 11

Nutrition: Fuel for the Machine 🥗

Your body is an athletic machine — and like every machine, it runs on fuel. The food you eat becomes the energy that powers your muscles, the building blocks that grow your bones, and the chemicals your brain uses to focus. Eat well, and your body has what it needs to perform. Eat poorly, and even the best training routine falls flat.

1
Lesson 1
The Three Macronutrients

Almost every food gives you a mix of three main macronutrients ("macro" = big). Each does a different job:

🍞
Carbohydrates
Your body's preferred fuel for movement. Found in grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy.
🍗
Proteins
Building blocks for muscles, bones, skin, blood. Found in meat, eggs, beans, dairy, nuts.
🥑
Fats
Long-lasting energy + protect your organs and brain. Found in oils, nuts, avocado, fish.

You need all three. Skipping any one — like cutting all fat or all carbs — leaves your body short on something important.

2
Lesson 2
Vitamins, Minerals, and Water

Macronutrients are the big ones, but your body also needs smaller amounts of micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — to function:

  • Vitamin C — helps your body heal cuts and fight off colds (citrus, peppers, strawberries)
  • Calcium — builds strong bones and teeth (milk, yogurt, leafy greens)
  • Iron — helps blood carry oxygen (red meat, beans, spinach)
  • Potassium — keeps muscles working properly and prevents cramps (bananas, potatoes)

And don't forget water. Your body is about 60% water. Even small amounts of dehydration can hurt your focus, mood, and performance.

🧪Sport Science

When you eat carbs, your body breaks them down into glucose — a simple sugar. Glucose either gets used right away as fuel, or stored in your muscles and liver as glycogen for later. During a long workout, your muscles tap into that glycogen storage. That's why athletes "carb load" before big events — they're topping off their fuel tanks.

3
Lesson 3
Eat the Rainbow

Different colored fruits and vegetables contain different vitamins. The more colors on your plate, the wider the range of nutrients you get:

🍎
Red
Tomatoes, strawberries, bell peppers — good for the heart.
🥕
Orange/Yellow
Carrots, oranges, sweet potatoes — vitamin A for eyes and skin.
🥦
Green
Broccoli, spinach, kale — vitamins and minerals galore.
🫐
Blue/Purple
Blueberries, eggplant, purple grapes — antioxidants for the brain.
🧄
White
Garlic, onions, cauliflower — immune system support.
💡Did You Know?

Your gut — the long tube that processes food — contains trillions of bacteria that help break down food and even talk to your brain. Scientists call this the "gut microbiome," and it's connected to your mood, immune system, and energy level. The way you build a healthy microbiome? Eat lots of different plants (fruits, veggies, beans, nuts). The more variety, the better.

4
Lesson 4
Building a Balanced Plate

The simplest tool for healthy eating is the MyPlate model from the U.S. Department of Agriculture:

  • ½ of your plate — fruits and vegetables
  • ¼ of your plate — grains (preferably whole grains)
  • ¼ of your plate — protein (meat, beans, nuts, eggs)
  • A side — dairy (milk, yogurt, cheese) or a calcium alternative

You don't have to be perfect at every meal. The goal is to look at most of your meals over a week and see balance.

🌎Real-World Connection

Pro athletes work with sports nutritionists who plan meals down to the gram. An NBA player might eat 4,000 calories a day during the season, carefully timed before, during, and after practice. Meanwhile, an Olympic gymnast might eat closer to 2,000 calories with extra protein and calcium for bone health. Different sports = different fuel needs.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Macronutrients — The three big nutrients your body needs in large amounts — carbs, protein, fat.
  • Micronutrients — Vitamins and minerals — needed in small amounts but still essential.
  • Carbohydrates — The body's main fuel source for movement.
  • Protein — Nutrient used to build and repair muscles.
  • Glycogen — Stored form of carbs that your muscles use as fuel (stretch term).
  • Dehydration — When your body doesn't have enough water to function well.
📝Weekly Reflection

What did you eat yesterday? List your meals and snacks. Which macronutrients did you get? Did you eat the rainbow? Pick one meal you'd change for better fuel, and explain why that change would help your body — what specific nutrient or system would benefit?

→What's Next

Next: build a healthy plate in Week 12, then power your Flight Club challenge with what you've learned.

5th Grade PE · Unit 1.7 · Locomotor Skills
Week 13

Locomotor Skills: Master How You Move 🏃

Every athletic skill starts with locomotion — moving your body from one place to another. There are eight basic locomotor skills, and they're the alphabet of athletic movement. Volleyball players, dancers, ninja-warrior racers, soccer goalkeepers — they all combine these eight patterns into something more complex. Master the basics, and the advanced moves get easier.

1
Lesson 1
The Eight Locomotor Skills

Coaches and PE teachers group movement into eight foundational patterns:

🚶
Walking
One foot always on the ground. Heel strikes first, toe pushes off.
🏃
Running
Both feet leave the ground briefly between steps.
🦘
Hopping
Push off and land on the SAME foot.
🤾
Jumping
Push off two feet, land on two feet.
🏃‍♀️
Galloping
One foot leads, the other catches up. Like a horse gait.
⏭️
Skipping
Step + hop, alternating sides. Step-hop, step-hop.
↔️
Sliding
Sideways movement — one foot leads, the other catches up.
🤸
Leaping
Push off one foot, land on the OTHER foot. Like jumping over a puddle.
🧪Sport Science

The brain region that controls locomotor patterns is called the motor cortex — a strip across the top of your brain. Every time you practice a movement, the connection between neurons (brain cells) gets a little stronger. After enough reps, the pattern becomes automatic — what athletes call "muscle memory." But it's not really stored in your muscles. It's stored in your brain.

2
Lesson 2
Why These Skills Matter

You probably already do most of these without thinking. So why practice them in PE?

Because in real games, you need to combine and switch between them. Soccer: jog, sprint, slide to defend, leap over a tackle. Basketball: shuffle on defense, gallop down the court, jump to rebound. Tag: run, change direction, slide, jump over an obstacle. The smoother your transitions between locomotor patterns, the more efficient and faster you are.

Athletes also have to do these skills under pressure — when they're tired, when an opponent is in the way, when the ground is uneven. Practicing the patterns deliberately makes them more reliable when the game gets messy.

3
Lesson 3
Coordination & Kinesthetic Awareness

Locomotor skills depend on kinesthetic awareness — your brain's ability to feel where your body is in space. Try this: close your eyes and touch your nose. You didn't see your finger, but you knew where it was. That's kinesthetic awareness.

Strong kinesthetic awareness lets you:

  • Land safely when jumping from a height
  • Avoid stepping on a teammate's foot
  • Adjust your stride mid-run to dodge an obstacle
  • Stay balanced on uneven ground
💡Did You Know?

Astronauts on the International Space Station have to re-learn walking when they come back to Earth. Without gravity, their kinesthetic awareness drifts — their brain forgets how heavy their body is. NASA has astronauts do special rehab to relearn locomotor patterns. It's a powerful reminder that even "automatic" skills are actually learned and maintained.

4
Try It
Locomotor Skill Circuit

Try this 4-minute circuit to practice all 8 patterns. Do each for 30 seconds:

  1. Walk forward, focusing on heel-to-toe motion
  2. Jog at a steady, controlled pace
  3. Hop on right foot — switch to left foot halfway
  4. Jump in place with two feet, knees soft on landing
  5. Gallop forward, then switch lead leg
  6. Skip with high knees
  7. Slide sideways — left direction, then right
  8. Leap forward over an imaginary line, focus on landing softly
🌎Real-World Connection

Track and field coaches use locomotor drills with even Olympic-level sprinters. Skipping (called "A-skips" and "B-skips"), high-knee runs, and side shuffles are part of every elite sprinter's warm-up. The basics never stop being useful — they just get more refined.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Locomotion — Moving your body from one place to another.
  • Locomotor skills — The 8 fundamental movement patterns: walk, run, hop, jump, gallop, skip, slide, leap.
  • Hop — Push off and land on the same foot.
  • Leap — Push off one foot, land on the other foot.
  • Kinesthetic awareness — Your brain's sense of where your body is in space (stretch term).
  • Motor cortex — The part of the brain that controls voluntary movement (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Which locomotor skill is your strongest? Which is the weakest? How do you know? Pick the skill you'd want to improve most, and explain how it would help in a specific sport, game, or activity you enjoy.

→What's Next

Week 15

Throwing & Catching: The Art of Sending and Receiving 🎯

Throwing and catching are manipulative skills — moves where your body controls an object instead of just moving itself. They look simple, but they involve a chain reaction of body parts: legs, hips, core, shoulder, elbow, wrist, fingers. When the chain is timed right, the ball flies fast and straight. When it's off, the ball flutters.

1
Lesson 1
The Mechanics of a Throw

A good overhand throw uses the entire body. The power doesn't come from your arm — it comes from the ground up. Here's the chain:

  1. Stand sideways — non-throwing shoulder pointing at the target
  2. Step toward the target with your opposite foot (right hand → step with left foot)
  3. Rotate your hips as your foot lands
  4. Drive your throwing shoulder forward as the hips finish rotating
  5. Whip your arm through — elbow leads, hand follows
  6. Snap your wrist on release for spin and accuracy
  7. Follow through — your hand should finish near your opposite hip

Every step in that chain transfers energy up to the next. Skip a step (like throwing all from your arm) and you lose most of your power.

🧪Sport Science

This chain is called the kinetic chain — energy moves from your feet through your legs, hips, core, shoulder, and out through your fingertips. Major League Baseball pitchers reach about 50% of their throwing speed from their legs and hips alone. The arm is just the last link. That's why pitchers do squats and core work — strong legs throw harder.

2
Lesson 2
Catching: Soft Hands and Quick Eyes

Catching looks like one skill, but it's actually three working together:

  • Tracking — keeping your eyes on the ball from leave-hand to arrival
  • Positioning — moving your body so the ball arrives in front of your chest
  • Receiving — using "soft hands" that give a little on impact so the ball doesn't bounce out

The hardest part for most kids is positioning. You have to move your feet — not just your arms. Great catchers are great mover-of-feet first, great hand-users second.

3
Lesson 3
Different Throws for Different Situations
🎯
Overhand Throw
Long distance, max power. Baseball, football, javelin.
🥎
Underhand Toss
Short distance, gentle arc. Softball pitch, bocce, beanbag toss.
🏀
Two-Handed Pass
Quick, accurate. Basketball chest pass, soccer throw-in.
⚾
Sidearm
Lower, faster release. Used for quick infield throws or skipping a stone.
💡Did You Know?

Humans are the only animals who can throw with both speed AND accuracy. Chimpanzees can throw, but only at about 20 mph and not very accurately. Your shoulder joint evolved a unique shape that lets you whip your arm fast — scientists think this gave early humans a huge survival advantage in hunting. So when you make a great throw, you're using a skill that's literally thousands of years old.

4
Try It
Throw & Catch Drills
🎯
Wall Throw
Throw against a wall, catch the rebound. 20 reps each hand.
🪣
Bucket Toss
Underhand toss into a bucket, 5 feet away. Move it back as you improve.
👥
Partner Catch
Throw and catch with a partner, 10 feet apart. Step with each throw.
🪞
Wall Catch
Toss ball up, catch with both hands. Then one hand. Then with a clap between!
🌎Real-World Connection

NFL quarterbacks throw a football about 60 mph with pinpoint accuracy on a moving target while being chased by 300-pound defenders. They train this skill thousands of reps a week. The same chain of movements you're learning — sideways stance, step, hip rotation, follow-through — is exactly what a Super Bowl winner uses, just with more practice.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Manipulative skills — Movement skills that involve controlling an object (ball, racket, bat).
  • Overhand throw — Throw with the arm coming over the shoulder — for distance and power.
  • Underhand toss — Throw with the arm swinging below the shoulder — for short, soft passes.
  • Kinetic chain — How energy transfers from feet through hips to the throwing arm (stretch term).
  • Follow-through — Completing the motion after releasing the ball — adds accuracy.
  • Soft hands — Hands that give a little on impact so a ball doesn't bounce out.
📝Weekly Reflection

What part of your throwing motion is weakest? Record yourself throwing (or have a partner watch). Check: do you step with the opposite foot? Do your hips rotate? Do you follow through? Pick the one piece to fix first — and explain why it matters in the kinetic chain.

→What's Next

  • Sit on the floor with feet together and knees bent outward.
  • Hold your feet with your hands and gently push your knees toward the floor.

  • Optional: Pretend your legs are butterfly wings and gently flap them!

Flamingo Stretch (Quadriceps Stretch)

  • Stand tall and bend one knee, bringing your foot behind you.
  • Hold your ankle with your hand and keep your balance.
  • Keep your knees close together and hold for 10 seconds.
  • Switch legs and repeat.
  • Optional: Extend one arm forward like a flamingo's neck!

Benefits: Stretches the front of the thigh (quadriceps) and improves balance.

🚀 Flight Club Challenge

Three strength moves that hit your legs, core, and arms. Locomotor skills depend on these muscle groups — this challenge builds the engine.

1
Split Squat
  1. Stand up tall with one foot in front and the other foot behind you — like you're about to take a big step.
  2. Keep your front knee over your ankle and your back heel lifted off the ground.
  3. Slowly bend both knees to lower your body straight down.
  4. Stop when your back knee is close to the ground (but not touching!).
  5. Stand back up. Do 5 slow squats, then switch legs and repeat.

Benefits: Makes your leg muscles stronger, especially your thighs and calves.

2
Superman Hold
  1. Lie flat on your stomach on the floor or a soft mat.
  2. Stretch your arms straight out in front of you and your legs straight behind you.
  3. At the same time, lift your arms, chest, and legs slightly off the ground.
  4. Try to hold this pose for 10 seconds — like you're flying through the sky!
  5. Slowly lower back down and rest. Try it again 2–3 more times!

Benefits: Strengthens your back and core muscles.

3
Bench Dips
  1. Find a sturdy chair, bench, or low table. Sit on the edge with your hands next to your hips.
  2. Walk your feet forward and slide your bottom off the edge, so your hands are holding you up.
  3. Bend your elbows to lower your body a little — like you're going down slowly.
  4. Push back up until your arms are straight again.
  5. Try doing 5–10 dips, then take a break!

Benefits: Strengthens your arms, shoulders, and chest.
